title: LSA Act ss. 20 & 21 — Award of Lok Adalat (Deemed Civil Court decree, non-appealable) (LSA Act ss. 20-21)

content.overview: Sections 20 and 21 of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 govern how a Lok Adalat takes cognizance and what an award does. For a pending case, the court may refer it if the parties agree, or if one party applies and the court is prima facie satisfied that settlement is possible, or if the court is satisfied that the matter is appropriate for the Lok Adalat. A pre-litigation matter may be referred by the Authority or Committee after hearing the other party. The Lok Adalat then attempts a compromise or settlement. If none is reached, the record returns to the court. Every Lok Adalat award is deemed a decree of a civil court or, where applicable, an order of any other court. It is final and binding, and no appeal lies against the award. Court-fee paid in a case referred under s. 20(1) is refunded under the Court-fees Act, 1870.
content.glance: LSA Act ss. 20 & 21 — Award of Lok Adalat (Deemed Civil Court decree, non-appealable) (LSA Act ss. 20-21). Complete ADR treatise with statutory deconstruction, examples, verified authorities, forum analysis and chamber drafting.
content.study: Separate the referral route (agreement, one-party application, court satisfaction, or pre-litigation reference after hearing) from the award consequence. An award exists only if compromise or settlement is arrived at. Finality and the no-appeal rule do not convert the Lok Adalat into an appellate court.

cases.facts: The Court considered arbitrability and the role of the referral court.
cases.issue: When should a court refer parties to arbitration and which disputes are non-arbitrable?
cases.ratioDecidendi: Referral scrutiny is limited, but the court must reject inherently non-arbitrable disputes and examine the arbitration agreement at the statutory threshold.

cases.name: Perkins Eastman Architects DPC v. HSCC (India) Ltd.
cases.facts: The dispute concerned unilateral appointment power vested in an interested party.
cases.issue: Whether a person interested in the outcome may unilaterally appoint the sole arbitrator.
cases.ratioDecidendi: A person rendered ineligible to act as arbitrator cannot control the appointment process in a manner that creates justifiable bias.
cases.holding: The unilateral appointment mechanism was held invalid in the circumstances.
cases.relevance: Use for independence, impartiality and appointment challenges.

enhancement.definition: Section 20 is the cognizance and referral provision. Section 21 gives a Lok Adalat award the status of a deemed civil-court decree or other-court order, makes it final and binding, bars an appeal, and refunds court-fee in a case referred under s. 20(1).
enhancement.legalPrinciple: The award is the record of a compromise or settlement, not an adjudicated judgment on evidence. Its enforceability comes from the deemed-decree rule, and its finality is statutory: no appeal lies to any court against the award.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, ss. 20 and 21; Court-fees Act, 1870 for refund; CPC execution follows from the deemed-decree status. Permanent Lok Adalat decision-on-merits is s. 22C, not s. 21.
essentialIngredients: Pending-case referral: party agreement, or one-party application with prima facie settlement chance, or court satisfaction that the matter is appropriate
Pre-litigation referral only after a reasonable hearing opportunity to the other party
Compromise or settlement actually arrived at
Award deemed a civil-court decree or other-court order
Final and binding; no appeal; court-fee refund for a s. 20(1) reference
If no settlement, record returned to the referring court
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 20(1) controls pending cases. Consent of both parties is one route, not the only route: a single party's application can lead to reference if the court is prima facie satisfied of a chance of settlement, and the court may also refer a matter it considers appropriate. Section 20(2) covers matters not yet before a court, but the other party must have a reasonable opportunity of being heard. Section 20(3) directs the Lok Adalat to dispose of the case or matter by compromise or settlement. Section 20(5) is the failure rule: no award, and the record goes back for disposal in accordance with law. Section 21(1) supplies the enforcement status and the court-fee refund. Section 21(2) supplies finality and the appeal bar. Do not describe the award as a reasoned adjudication on contested evidence.
examples: Both parties in a pending recovery suit agree to a Lok Adalat reference; a settlement award follows and court-fee is refundable.
One party applies, the court is prima facie satisfied, and the suit is referred; if talks fail, the record returns under s. 20(5).
A pre-litigation reference is attempted without hearing the other side; s. 20(2) proviso is not met.
The award-holder seeks execution as a deemed decree; the other side files an appeal against the award, which s. 21(2) bars.
enhancement.problemApplication: Identify the referral subsection; check hearing if pre-litigation; ask whether a compromise was actually signed; if yes, apply deemed-decree, finality, no-appeal and refund; if no, return the record. Do not invent a merits judgment.
distinctions: Referral under s. 20 vs award under s. 21
Deemed decree vs a contested civil judgment
Ordinary Lok Adalat award vs Permanent Lok Adalat determination on merits under s. 22C
No appeal under s. 21(2) vs execution of the deemed decree

keyTakeaways: Consent of both parties is sufficient but not the only referral route for a pending case.
No settlement means no award and return of the record.
The award is deemed a decree or other-court order.
It is final and binding and no appeal lies against it.
Court-fee refund applies to a case referred under s. 20(1).
